questions.question: Why does the aggregator require every input score to be in [0, 1]?
options: Without a common scale, a single metric reported on a 0-100 range would dominate the per-model mean
The [0, 1] range happens to be the same bin range used by the expected-calibration-error computation
The numpy library internally requires all array values to fall within the [0, 1] range to function
The markdown table renderer expects every score to be formatted with exactly two decimal places
questions.explanation: If pass-rate is in [0,1] and BLEU is in [0,100], the latter swamps the average. Normalisation belongs at the metric layer and is checked here.

questions.question: What information does mean score hide that win-rate exposes?
options: Whether the model's predicted confidence scores are well calibrated against actual outcomes
The raw number of tasks the model actually completed during the full evaluation run
The width of the bootstrap confidence interval computed around the headline mean score
Per-task wins resist outliers and scale shifts; the mean is sensitive to both of those
questions.explanation: Win-rate counts task-by-task wins. A model can have a high mean from one easy task and still lose most pairwise comparisons.

questions.question: How does bootstrap_mean_ci estimate the confidence interval?
options: By assuming the sample mean follows a normal distribution and using its analytic standard error term
By resampling task scores with replacement and taking the alpha/2 and 1-alpha/2 percentiles of the means
By computing the standard deviation of the scores analytically and deriving a symmetric interval around it
By calling out to scipy.stats.bootstrap and using its default percentile-method configuration
questions.explanation: Non-parametric percentile bootstrap on the per-task scores; no distributional assumption, no scipy.

questions.question: When does the pairwise diff CI report `significant`?
options: When the raw mean difference between the two models is larger than an absolute threshold of 0.1
When both models being compared have completed more than thirty tasks in the evaluation
When the confidence interval around the difference does not contain zero at all
When the two models' win-rates against each other happen to be numerically unequal
questions.explanation: A CI that strictly excludes zero means the difference is unlikely to be zero at the chosen level; that is the operational definition the lesson uses.

questions.question: Why is the pairwise bootstrap paired rather than independent?
options: Paired bootstrap respects that the same task feeds both models; differences are computed per task
Independent bootstrap sampling is not something the Python language is able to express at all
Paired bootstrap happens to run measurably faster than an independent bootstrap would on the same data
Paired bootstrap is the only bootstrap variant that the numpy library provides support for
questions.explanation: Paired bootstrap reduces noise: we sample over tasks, not over models, so the comparison is on the same task set every iteration.

questions.question: Why does the aggregator return per-category means alongside the headline number?
options: Returning per-category means is a requirement imposed by the JSON Schema the leaderboard record follows
Computing per-category means happens to run faster than computing a single overall mean across categories
The markdown table renderer requires a per-category breakdown in order to render the leaderboard at all
Headline mean can mask category-level weakness (good overall, bad at code); per-category exposes that
questions.explanation: A model can win on aggregate by being okay everywhere or by dominating one category. Per-category breakdown lets the consumer see which.
